PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money.
Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs.
A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections.
Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.

***Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns.*** Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.

Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
***Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs.*** Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers.

Proposition 89 
Proposition 89, an initiative measure which appeared on the November 7, 2006 General 
Election ballot, was defeated by an almost 3-1 margin.
Proposition 89 would have enacted a “clean money” system of campaign financing similar to those currently in place in Arizona and Maine.
Under “clean money,” participating candidates would qualify for large amounts of public funds to expend on their campaigns once they collect a threshold amount of small ($5) qualifying contributions.
Once qualified, candidates could not raise or spend campaign funds from any other source other than the “clean money” (with limited exceptions).
Proposition 89 also lowered the current limit on contributions that non-participating candidates may accept and placed restrictions on direct corporate contributions to initiative campaigns.
Proposition 89 would have funded the “clean money” system by raising roughly $200 million per year through an increase in the current income tax on corporations and specified financial institutions.
Proposition 15 
Proposition 15, another “clean money” system was placed on the June, 2010 ballot by the

### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).

The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974, prohibits a public officer from expending, and a candidate from accepting, public moneys for the purpose of seeking elective office.
This bill would remove prohibitions imposed on a public officer or candidate to expend or accept public funds, as defined, for the purpose of seeking elective office unless the funds are earmarked by a state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety.

The bill would prohibit public funds from being used to pay legal defense fees or fines or to repay personal loans to their campaign.

### Additional Titles

### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).
SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns.
The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.
Gov.
Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future.
The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns.
Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements.

This act repeals the ban on public funding of political campaigns.
Creates a voluntary system for candidates for Secretary of State to qualify for a public campaign grant if they agree to limitations on spending and private contributions.
Candidates would have to qualify before receiving the grant.

### Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (SB 42).
SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns.
The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025.
Gov.
Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future.
